We keep shen as "self" throughout the chapter, since its whole argument turns on the self you exhaust in chasing name and wealth — and we render the questions as plain, bare comparisons so they land as the original means them to, blunt and personal.

divergences.locus: the close (知足不辱，知止不殆)
divergences.phrase: Know what is enough ... Know when to stop
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "Who is content / Needs fear no shame. / Who knows to stop / Incurs no blame. / From danger free / Long live shall he."
divergences.lectio: Know what is enough, and you meet no disgrace. Know when to stop, and you meet no danger. And so you endure.
divergences.note: The two matched maxims are zhi zu (知足), to know sufficiency — to know when you have enough — and zhi zhi (知止), to know when to stop. Legge keeps the sense but breaks it into a sing-song verse and softens dai (殆), real danger or peril, into mere "blame." We restore the pairing as two plain imperatives and keep dai as "danger," so the chapter's last turn holds: the one who knows enough and knows when to halt is never disgraced, never imperiled, and so 長久 — lasts long, endures.

divergences.phrase: Movement overcomes the cold; stillness overcomes the heat.
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "Constant action overcomes cold; being still overcomes heat."
divergences.lectio: Movement overcomes the cold; stillness overcomes the heat.
divergences.note: The Chinese is 躁勝寒，靜勝熱. 躁 (zào) means restless, hurried movement — the bodily fact that stirring about warms you against the cold, while keeping still cools you in the heat. Legge's "constant action" reaches for a moral abstraction the line does not carry; we keep the plain, physical image, which lets the closing turn — that it is purity and stillness, not restless motion, that truly sets the world right — land as the quiet reversal the chapter intends.

divergences.phrase: There is no calamity greater than not knowing when you have enough; there is no fault greater than the craving to get more.
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "There is no guilt greater than to sanction ambition; no calamity greater than to be discontented with one's lot; no fault greater than the wish to be getting."
divergences.lectio: There is no calamity greater than not knowing when you have enough; there is no fault greater than the craving to get more.
divergences.note: The received Chinese gives two parallel lines, 禍莫大於不知足，咎莫大於欲得 — "no calamity greater than not knowing contentment, no fault greater than the craving to get." Legge prefaced these with a third clause, "no guilt greater than to sanction ambition," which follows a variant text (罪莫大於可欲) and reads 可欲 as endorsing ambition. We keep the two lines of the standard text, the pairing nearly all modern versions share, because the chapter's whole point is the single failing of wanting more — to which discontent and grasping are the two faces.

divergences.phrase: The farther you go, the less you know.
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "The farther that one goes out (from himself), the less he knows."
divergences.lectio: The farther you go, the less you know.
divergences.note: The Chinese is 其出弥远，其知弥少 — literally "the more one goes out, the less one knows." Legge added the parenthetical "(from himself)," reading the line as a soul straying from its own center. The text simply opposes outward travel to inward knowing, picking up the door and the window of the lines before, so we keep the plain contrast: the more you chase knowledge by going abroad, the less you truly understand.

divergences.locus: the turn to wu wei (損之又損，以至於無為)
divergences.phrase: until you come to acting without forcing. Act without forcing, and nothing is left undone.
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "He diminishes it and again diminishes it, till he arrives at doing nothing (on purpose). Having arrived at this point of non-action, there is nothing which he does not do."
divergences.lectio: Dropped, and dropped again, until you come to acting without forcing. Act without forcing, and nothing is left undone.
divergences.note: The hinge is wu wei (無為), the book's central paradox: 損之又損，以至於無為，無為而無不為. Legge's "doing nothing (on purpose)" reads as inertia, which misses the point — wu wei is not idleness but action that does not strain against the grain of things. We render it as acting-without-forcing, consistent with the rest of the edition, so the paradox lands: precisely by ceasing to push, nothing is left undone (無不為).

divergences.locus: winning the world (取天下常以無事)
divergences.phrase: The world is always won by leaving it alone. Once you start to meddle, you are not fit to win the world.
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "He who gets as his own all under heaven does so by giving himself no trouble (with that end). If one take trouble (with that end), he is not equal to getting as his own all under heaven."
divergences.lectio: The world is always won by leaving it alone. Once you start to meddle, you are not fit to win the world.
divergences.note: The Chinese 取天下常以無事，及其有事，不足以取天下 turns on wu shi (無事), "no business, no fuss," against you shi (有事), getting busy, interfering. Legge's "giving himself no trouble" reads as personal ease, but the point is political and active: tian xia (天下), the world, is won by not meddling in it, and the moment you start to interfere you forfeit it. We keep "leaving it alone" and "meddle" so the chapter's lesson echoes the wu wei it has just named — the world comes to the hand that does not grasp.

divergences.locus: opening line (聖人無常心，以百姓心為心)
divergences.phrase: The sage has no fixed mind of his own; he takes the mind of the people as his own.
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "The sage has no invariable mind of his own; he makes the mind of the people his mind."
divergences.lectio: The sage has no fixed mind of his own; he takes the mind of the people as his own.
divergences.note: The Chinese 聖人無常心，以百姓心為心 turns on chang xin (常心), the constant, fixed, settled mind one clings to as one's own. The sage empties himself of any such private agenda and lets the mind of the bai xing (百姓), the common people, become his. Legge's "invariable mind" is faithful but stiff; "fixed mind" keeps the sense of a rigid, preset self while reading plainly, and we let the second half stand as a clean parallel rather than Legge's flatter "makes the mind of the people his mind."

divergences.locus: winning goodness and trust (德善 / 德信)
divergences.phrase: and so goodness is won ... and so trust is won
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "and thus (all) get to be good ... and thus (all) get to be sincere."
divergences.lectio: and so goodness is won ... and so trust is won
divergences.note: The refrain is de shan (德善) and de xin (德信). De (德) here works as the verb "to get, to gain, to win" (a common loan for 得), so the lines say that by meeting bad with good and distrust with trust, the sage gains goodness itself and gains trust itself — they are produced in the world by his refusal to mirror them. Legge reads de as a passive "get to be" spread over "all," which is defensible but diffuse. We keep the active turn — goodness is won, trust is won — so the paradox lands: you do not coax goodness out of people by judging them, you bring it into being by being good to them first. We render xin (信) as "trust" rather than Legge's "sincere," since the chapter is about the bond of trust between ruler and people, not inward sincerity alone.

divergences.phrase: Three in ten are companions of life. Three in ten are companions of death.
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "Of every ten three are ministers of life (to themselves); and three are ministers of death."
divergences.lectio: Three in ten are companions of life. Three in ten are companions of death.
divergences.note: The Chinese is 生之徒十有三，死之徒十有三. The phrase 十有三 can be read "three out of ten" (Legge, Wang Bi) or "thirteen" — the old commentator Heshang Gong took the latter, counting the four limbs and nine openings of the body as the thirteen avenues of both life and death. We follow the "three in ten" reading shared by most modern scholars, since the chapter is sorting people into kinds, not listing parts of the body. 徒 (tú) means a follower or companion of, which we keep over Legge's "ministers."

divergences.phrase: Because in him there is no room for death.
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "Because there is in him no place of death."
divergences.lectio: Because in him there is no room for death.
divergences.note: The closing line is 以其無死地 — literally "because he has no death-ground." 地 (dì) is the same "ground" or "place" that the rhino, tiger, and blade are each said to find no 所 (place) of. The point is spatial: there is nowhere in him for death to take hold. "No room for death" carries that better in modern English than Legge's flat "place of death," which can be misread as a location one travels to rather than an opening within the man.

divergences.phrase: its virtue nurtures them
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "and nourished by its outflowing operation" (德, de, rendered as "its outflowing operation")
divergences.lectio: and its virtue nurtures them
divergences.note: The chapter is built on a pair: 道生之，德畜之 — the Way (道, dào) gives life, and de (德) nurtures. De is the te the book is named for, the inner power the Way lends to each thing so that it can grow into itself. Legge renders de here as "its outflowing operation," an abstraction that hides the key word and breaks the link to Chapter 10 and Chapter 38, where the same de appears. We render it "virtue" — its older English sense of the active power in a thing, not mere goodness — so the reader hears the book's title word and feels the two forces work as one: the Way bears each thing, its virtue feeds it.

divergences.phrase: It is always so of itself.
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "is not the result of any ordination, but always a spontaneous tribute."
divergences.lectio: It is commanded by no one. It is always so of itself.
divergences.note: The line is 夫莫之命而常自然. 自然 (zìrán) is the book's great word — "so of itself," what is the case naturally, without being forced or decreed (the same word the people speak in Chapter 17). Legge's "a spontaneous tribute" adds a note of homage the bare phrase does not carry. We keep zìrán plain — the honor things pay the Way is not handed down by command but rises of itself — so the chapter's quiet point lands: the Way is revered not because it rules, but because reverence is simply natural to things that owe it their being.

divergences.phrase: Stop up the openings, shut the gates, and to the end of your days your strength will never run out.
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "Let him keep his mouth closed, and shut up the portals (of his nostrils), and all his life he will be exempt from laborious exertion."
divergences.lectio: Stop up the openings, shut the gates, and to the end of your days your strength will never run out.
divergences.note: The Chinese is 塞其兌，閉其門，終身不勤. 兌 (duì) literally means an aperture or opening, and Legge fixed it as the mouth, with 門 (mén, "gate") read narrowly as the nostrils. But the image is deliberately general — the senses and desires as openings through which a person's vitality drains out. Reading it as "the mouth" alone narrows a figure that the rest of the chapter (the inner light, the soft) keeps wide open. 不勤 we render "never run out (of strength)" rather than Legge's "exempt from laborious exertion": the point is undepleted vitality, not avoiding hard work.

divergences.phrase: This is the robber's boast, not the Way.
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "such (princes) may be called robbers and boasters. This is contrary to the Tao surely!"
divergences.lectio: This is the robber's boast, not the Way.
divergences.note: The Chinese is 是謂盜夸 (shì wèi dào kuā) — literally "this is called the robber's boast." 夸 (kuā) is boasting, swagger, showing off; the phrase paints a ruler who lives in plundered luxury and then flaunts it. Legge splits it into two nouns, "robbers and boasters," but it is one image: the swagger of theft. We keep it as a single sharp phrase, and let the contrast with the Way land in the same breath rather than as a separate exclamation.

divergences.locus: opening line (善建者不拔，善抱者不脫)
divergences.phrase: What is well planted cannot be uprooted. What is firmly held cannot slip away.
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "What (Tao's) skilful planter plants / Can never be uptorn; / What his skilful arms enfold, / From him can ne'er be borne."
divergences.lectio: What is well planted cannot be uprooted. What is firmly held cannot slip away.
divergences.note: The Chinese 善建者不拔，善抱者不脫 is a matched pair: shan jian (善建, well built or well planted) that bu ba (不拔, cannot be pulled up), and shan bao (善抱, firmly embraced or held) that bu tuo (不脫, cannot slip free). Legge spins it into a rhyming quatrain about a "skilful planter" and arms that "enfold," which is faithful in spirit but buries the two bare proverbs under Victorian verse. We keep them as the plain, parallel sayings the chapter opens with — what is rooted deeply stays, what is held truly does not get away — since the rest of the chapter is built on that image of a power planted so deep it cannot be torn out.

divergences.locus: the scaling of power (修之於身…其德乃真 … 修之於天下…其德乃普)
divergences.phrase: Cultivate the Way in yourself, and your power becomes real... Cultivate it in the world, and its power reaches everywhere.
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "Tao when nursed within one's self, / His vigour will make true; / And where the family it rules / What riches will accrue!..."
divergences.lectio: Cultivate the Way in yourself, and your power becomes real. Cultivate it in the family, and its power overflows. Cultivate it in the village, and its power endures. Cultivate it in the state, and its power abounds. Cultivate it in the world, and its power reaches everywhere.
divergences.note: The Chinese is a five-rung ladder, each rung repeating xiu zhi (修之, cultivate it) and qi de (其德, its de) across a widening circle — self, family, village, state, world — and naming what the de becomes at each scale: zhen (真, genuine, real), yu (餘, overflowing surplus), chang (長, lasting), feng (豐, abundant), pu (普, universal, everywhere). De (德) is the te the book is named for, which we render "power" throughout. Legge unrolls the chant into a rhyming verse of "vigour," "riches," and "good fortune" that loses both the repeated frame and the precise word at each step. We keep the parallel "cultivate it… and its power…" so the reader feels the same thing widen outward, the cultivated power growing truer at the root and broader at the reach.

divergences.locus: opening line (含德之厚，比於赤子)
divergences.phrase: One full of virtue is like a newborn child.
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "He who has in himself abundantly the attributes (of the Tao) is like an infant."
divergences.lectio: One full of virtue is like a newborn child.
divergences.note: The Chinese is 含德之厚，比於赤子. De (德) is the te the book is named for — the inner power of the Way, which we render "virtue" throughout the edition, in its old sense of the power proper to a thing (cf. Chapters 38, 51). Legge unpacks it into "the attributes (of the Tao)," which is faithful but clutters the line and hides the single word the chapter turns on. The child is 赤子 (chizi), literally the "red child," the newborn still flushed at birth; we keep "newborn child" so the image lands plain and the chapter opens on the one figure it is built around — the infant whose softness is its safety.

divergences.locus: the close (物壯則老，謂之不道，不道早已)
divergences.phrase: what is against the Way comes early to its end
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "When things have become strong, they (then) become old, which may be said to be contrary to the Tao. Whatever is contrary to the Tao soon ends."
divergences.lectio: Things in their full strength grow old. This is what it means to be against the Way, and what is against the Way comes early to its end.
divergences.note: These three lines (物壯則老，謂之不道，不道早已) close the chapter, and they close Chapter 30 word for word — the book quoting itself. Legge's "may be said to be contrary to the Tao" and "soon ends" are accurate but loosen the bare, hammered repetition of bu dao (不道), "against the Way," struck twice in a row. We keep the doubled phrase and render the line exactly as we did in Chapter 30, so the reader hears the echo: forcing a thing to its peak only hurries it toward age and end, and that hurrying is itself the turning away from the Way.

divergences.phrase: This is called the mysterious union.
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "he will attemper his brightness, and bring himself into agreement with the obscurity (of others). This is called 'the Mysterious Agreement.'"
divergences.lectio: soften the glare, settle into the dust. This is called the mysterious union.
divergences.note: The Chinese names the state 玄同 (xuán tóng) — xuan, the deep mystery that runs through the whole book, joined to tong, sameness or merging. The sage who blunts his own sharpness and dims his own light no longer stands apart from things but is leveled into them, one with the common dust. Legge's "Mysterious Agreement" reads like a treaty; we keep "the mysterious union" so the word lands as it does in the Chinese — a merging into the whole, not a bargain struck with it. The two lines it caps, 和其光，同其塵 (soften the glare, share the dust), are the book's own image for this sameness, which is why the chapter names it xuan tong.

divergences.locus: block the openings, shut the gates (塞其兌，閉其門)
divergences.phrase: Block the openings, shut the gates.
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "He (who knows it) will keep his mouth shut and close the portals (of his nostrils)."
divergences.lectio: Block the openings, shut the gates.
divergences.note: The Chinese 塞其兌，閉其門 is the same pair that opens Chapter 52: dui (兌), the openings or apertures of the senses, and men (門), the gates through which the world rushes in. Legge pins them to specific body parts — "his mouth," "the portals (of his nostrils)" — which narrows a deliberately open image. We keep the bare "openings" and "gates," matching the Lectio rendering in Chapter 52, so the chapter reads as it means: close off the channels of grasping and noise, and the inner stillness holds.

divergences.locus: opening line (以正治國，以奇用兵，以無事取天下)
divergences.phrase: win the world by not meddling
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "the kingdom is made one's own (only) by freedom from action and purpose."
divergences.lectio: Govern the state with what is straight and ordinary. Wage war with surprise. But win the world by not meddling.
divergences.note: The Chinese sets three methods against each other: govern (治國) by 正 (zhèng, the upright, the straight, the normal); fight (用兵) by 奇 (qí, the irregular, the unexpected, surprise); but take the world (取天下) by 無事 (wú shì), literally "no-business," not stirring things up. Legge renders 正 as "correction" and 奇 as "crafty dexterity," which obscures the deliberate pairing of the straight against the surprising. We keep the three as a tight contrast and render 無事 as "not meddling" — the same leave-it-alone restraint as wu wei (acting-without-forcing), applied to ruling the whole world.

divergences.locus: the sharp weapons line (民多利器，國家滋昏)
divergences.phrase: The more sharp weapons the people have, the deeper the state falls into disorder.
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "the more implements to add to their profit that the people have, the greater disorder is there in the state and clan."
divergences.lectio: The more sharp weapons the people have, the deeper the state falls into disorder.
divergences.note: The crux is 利器 (lì qì). Legge reads it as "implements to add to their profit" — tools of gain — but in this list of escalations (prohibitions, weapons, cunning, laws) 利器 is most naturally the sharp weapon, the keen-edged instrument, which breeds the 昏 (hūn, darkness, disorder) that follows. We take 利器 as "sharp weapons," the reading that fits the chapter's argument that more force in private hands means more chaos for the state, not more prosperity.

divergences.locus: the sage's refrain (我無為而民自化 ... 我無欲而民自樸)
divergences.phrase: I act without forcing, and the people transform themselves ... the people return on their own to the uncarved block
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "I will do nothing (of purpose), and the people will be transformed of themselves ... I will manifest no ambition, and the people will of themselves attain to the primitive simplicity."
divergences.lectio: I act without forcing, and the people transform themselves. I love stillness, and the people right themselves. I do not meddle, and the people grow prosperous on their own. I have no desires, and the people return on their own to the uncarved block.
divergences.note: The close is four matched lines, each pairing the sage's restraint with the people's 自 (zì, of themselves, on their own): 無為 (wú wéi, acting-without-forcing) yields self-transforming; 好靜 (loving stillness) yields self-righting; 無事 (not-meddling) yields self-enriching; 無欲 (no desires) yields a return to 樸 (pǔ). Legge's "do nothing (of purpose)" reads as idleness and misses wu wei, and he dissolves 樸 into "the primitive simplicity." We keep wu wei as acting-without-forcing and restore 樸 as "the uncarved block," the book's standing image for unworked, original simplicity, so the chapter ends on the emblem Laozi returns to throughout.

divergences.locus: the famous reversal (禍兮福之所倚，福兮禍之所伏)
divergences.phrase: Misfortune is what fortune leans on; fortune is where misfortune hides.
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "Misery!—happiness is to be found by its side! Happiness!—misery lurks beneath it!"
divergences.lectio: Misfortune is what fortune leans on; fortune is where misfortune hides.
divergences.note: The Chinese 禍兮福之所倚，福兮禍之所伏 is the book's most quoted line, and it turns on two precise verbs: 倚 (yǐ), to lean on or rest against, and 伏 (fú), to lie hidden, to crouch in wait. Each of the pair, fortune (福) and misfortune (禍), is bound up inside the other — disaster is the very thing good luck props itself against, and good luck is the den where disaster lies low. Legge's exclamatory "Misery!—happiness is to be found by its side!" keeps the sense but breaks the line into Victorian outbursts and loses the quiet, structural reciprocity. We keep the two clauses balanced and bare, with leaning and hiding intact, so the proverb lands as it does in Chinese: neither state is ever pure or final, each already carrying its opposite folded inside.

divergences.locus: the close (方而不割，廉而不劌，直而不肆，光而不燿)
divergences.phrase: square-edged but cuts no one, sharp-cornered but wounds no one, straight but never severe, bright but not dazzling
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "the sage is (like) a square which cuts no one (with its angles); (like) a corner which injures no one (with its sharpness). He is straightforward, but allows himself no license; he is bright, but does not dazzle."
divergences.lectio: So the sage is square-edged but cuts no one, sharp-cornered but wounds no one, straight but never severe, bright but not dazzling.
divergences.note: The chapter ends in four matched clauses, each a quality that could harm held back from harming: 方而不割 (square, yet does not cut), 廉而不劌 (sharp-cornered, yet does not gash — 廉 is the keen edge or angle of a thing, 劌 to wound on it), 直而不肆 (straight, yet not unbridled), 光而不燿 (bright, yet does not dazzle). Legge unrolls the first two into bracketed similes ("like a square which cuts no one (with its angles)") that slow the drumbeat and clutter the parallel; his "allows himself no license" for 不肆 reaches for a moral gloss the spare Chinese does not spell out. We keep all four as tight, parallel pairs so the rhythm holds and the point stands clear: the sage has every edge — squareness, sharpness, straightness, brightness — yet turns none of it against others. The last clause, "bright but not dazzling" (光而不燿), is the line the chapter is remembered for, and we keep it nearly word for word.

divergences.locus: the two kinds of rule (其政悶悶，其民淳淳；其政察察，其民缺缺)
divergences.phrase: When the government is dull and unobtrusive, the people stay honest and whole.
divergences.older: Legge (1891), in verse: "The government that seems the most unwise, / Oft goodness to the people best supplies; / That which is meddling, touching everything, / Will work but ill, and disappointment bring."
divergences.lectio: When the government is dull and unobtrusive, the people stay honest and whole. When the government is sharp and prying, the people grow crafty and broken.
divergences.note: The Chinese is two flat parallel couplets: 其政悶悶 (a government 悶悶, muffled, dim, leaving things alone) yields 其民淳淳 (people 淳淳, simple, honest, unspoiled); 其政察察 (a government 察察, sharp-eyed, scrutinizing, prying into everything) yields 其民缺缺 (people 缺缺, deficient, cunning, broken). Legge dissolves the whole into a rhyming Victorian quatrain that adds judgments ("seems the most unwise," "meddling") and loses the bare cause-and-effect mirror. We restore the two plain conditionals so the contrast lands as the original sets it up — the quieter the rule, the wholer the people; the more intrusive the rule, the more crooked they become — which is also what sets up the chapter's turn into fortune and misfortune feeding on each other.

divergences.phrase: nothing is better than restraint
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "For regulating the human (in our constitution) and rendering the (proper) service to the heavenly, there is nothing like moderation."
divergences.lectio: In governing people and in serving heaven, nothing is better than restraint.
divergences.note: The crux is se (嗇), which Legge softens to "moderation" and pads with brackets — "the human (in our constitution)," "the (proper) service." Se is sharper and more concrete: it is the frugality of the careful farmer or steward, sparing what you have, husbanding your strength, not spending yourself out. Legge himself glosses it as the opposite of "living fast" and "burning the candle at both ends." We render it "restraint" (the sparing, hoarding economy of energy) and strip the scaffolding so the bare counsel stands: in ruling others and in serving heaven alike, there is nothing like holding back.

divergences.locus: the early yielding (夫唯嗇，是謂早服)
divergences.phrase: by restraint you yield early to the Way
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "It is only by this moderation that there is effected an early return (to man's normal state)."
divergences.lectio: It is only by restraint that you yield early to the Way.
divergences.note: The phrase is zao fu (早服). Fu (服) carries the senses of submitting, yielding, and giving oneself over — and by extension preparing in good time. Legge reads it as an "early return (to man's normal state)," supplying a destination the bare words do not name. We keep fu as an early yielding or submitting to the Way: the one who spares himself bends to the grain of things early, before he is forced to, and so begins gathering te (德, virtue, power) before any crisis comes — which is exactly the "deep store of power" the next line builds on.

divergences.phrase: the spirits of the dead lose their power to haunt
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "the manes of the departed will not manifest their spiritual energy."
divergences.lectio: the spirits of the dead lose their power to haunt
divergences.note: The Chinese is 以道赋天下，其鬼不神. 鬼 (guǐ) are the ghosts or spirits of the dead, and 神 (shén) is used here as a verb — to act as a spirit, to work uncanny, supernatural power. Legge's "manes" (a Latin word for the souls of the dead) and "manifest their spiritual energy" are accurate but archaic to the point of obscurity. We keep the plain image the chapter intends: when the Way governs, the dead no longer trouble the living, not because they are powerless but because their power is turned aside from doing harm.

divergences.locus: their power flows back to the people
divergences.phrase: the power of each flows back and gathers in the people
divergences.older: Legge (1891): "their good influences converge in the virtue (of the Tao)."
divergences.lectio: the power of each flows back and gathers in the people
divergences.note: The closing line is 夫兩不相傷，故德交歸焉. The word is 德 (dé, te) — virtue, the quiet power of acting without forcing — and 交歸 means it crosses over and returns, gathers and comes home. Legge folded the destination into "the virtue (of the Tao)," but most readers take 焉 (yān, "there, in that") to point at the people, who are where both the spirits' restraint and the sage's restraint converge. We name that resting place plainly: when neither the unseen powers nor the ruler do harm, the te of each settles back into the people themselves.

segments.text: The Way that can be spoken is not the eternal Way. The name that can be named is not the eternal name.
Nameless, it is the origin of heaven and earth. Named, it is the mother of all things.
So if you are always without desire, you see its hidden depths; but if desire is always in you, you see only its outer edges.
These two spring from the same source, though we call them by different names. Together they are the Mystery — mystery within mystery, the gate of all that is subtle and wonderful.
When everyone in the world recognizes beauty as beauty, ugliness has already appeared. When everyone recognizes good as good, what is not good has already appeared.

So it is that being and non-being give rise to each other; the difficult and the easy complete each other; the long and the short measure each other; the high and the low lean on each other; note and voice harmonize with each other; before and after follow each other. This is how it always is.
And so the sage goes about the work without forcing it, and teaches without using words.
All things arise, and the sage does not turn any away. They are brought to life, and the sage claims nothing as his own. The work is done, and he does not rest in it as an achievement.
It is just because he does not rest in it that the credit never leaves him.

Do not make a show of honoring the worthy, and the people will not compete with one another. Do not prize goods that are hard to come by, and the people will not turn to theft. Do not put on display the things that stir desire, and the heart of the people will stay calm.

And so, when the sage governs, he empties their minds and fills their bellies, weakens their ambition and strengthens their bones. He keeps the people free of cunning and free of craving, so that the clever ones never dare to force their hand. Act without forcing, and nothing is left ungoverned.
The Way is empty, yet however much you use it, it is never used up. It is so deep — the wellspring from which the ten thousand things flow.
It blunts the sharp edges, unties the knots, softens the glare, settles down with the dust. So still, so hidden, and yet it is always there.
I do not know whose child it is. It seems to be older than God.
Heaven and earth are not humane: they treat the ten thousand things as straw dogs. The sage is not humane: he treats the people as straw dogs.
The space between heaven and earth — is it not like a bellows? Empty, yet it never runs out; work it, and it gives out all the more.
Too many words run dry. Better to keep to the center.
The valley spirit never dies. It is called the mysterious female.
The gateway of the mysterious female is called the root of heaven and earth.
Faint and unbroken, it seems always to be there; draw on it, and it is never used up.
Heaven lasts, and earth endures. The reason heaven and earth can last and endure is that they do not live for themselves, and so they go on living.
And so the sage puts himself last, and finds himself out in front; he sets himself aside, and so is kept safe. Is it not because he is selfless that his own self is fulfilled?
The highest good is like water. Water benefits all things and does not contend with them; it settles in the low places that everyone else scorns. And so it is close to the Way.

In where it dwells, it holds to the ground. In the heart, it holds to depth. In giving, it holds to kindness. In speech, it holds to truth. In governing, it holds to good order. In handling affairs, it holds to skill. In moving, it holds to the right moment.
It is just because it does not contend that it is without fault.
Keep filling a cup to the brim, and you would have done better to stop in time. Hammer a blade to its sharpest edge, and the edge will not last.
Fill your hall with gold and jade, and no one can keep them safe. Grow proud of wealth and rank, and you bring ruin on yourself.
When the work is done and your name is rising, withdraw. This is the Way of heaven.

Can you hold body and soul in a single embrace and never let them part? Can you gather your breath and make it soft and supple, soft as a newborn child's? Can you cleanse the dark mirror of your mind until it is without a flaw?

Can you love the people and govern the state, and do it without scheming? When the gate of heaven opens and shuts, can you keep to the female, the yielding, receptive part? Can your understanding reach into every corner, and yet seem to know nothing at all?
To give life and to nourish it; to give life and not possess it; to do the work and not lay claim to it; to lead, and not to lord it over what you lead — this is what is called the mysterious power.
Thirty spokes meet at a single hub, but it is the hole at the center, where there is nothing, that makes the wheel of use.
Clay is shaped into a pot, but it is the hollow inside, where there is nothing, that makes the pot of use.
Doors and windows are cut to make a room, but it is the empty space within, where there is nothing, that makes the room of use.
So what is there gives advantage; what is not there gives use.

The five colors blind the eye. The five notes deafen the ear. The five flavors numb the palate. Racing and hunting drive the heart wild, and goods that are hard to come by knock a life off its course.
And so the sage goes by the belly, not the eye. He lets the one go and takes hold of the other.
Favor and disgrace are both alarming. Honor great trouble as you honor your own body.

What does it mean that favor and disgrace are both alarming? Favor is a thing from above, and to win it is to dread losing it; to lose it is to dread something worse. This is what it means that favor and disgrace are both alarming. And what does it mean to honor great trouble as you honor your own body? The reason I can suffer great trouble is that I have a body; if I had no body, what trouble could reach me?
So the one who honors the world as their own body can be given the world to hold; the one who loves the world as their own body can be trusted with the world.

Look for it, and you do not see it: call it the Unseen. Listen for it, and you do not hear it: call it the Unheard. Reach for it, and you cannot hold it: call it the Unfelt. These three cannot be pried apart and questioned one by one, so we blend them together and they are One.

Its upper side is not bright, its lower side is not dark. Unbroken, ceaseless, it cannot be named, and it returns again into nothing. This is the form of the formless, the image of what has no thing in it. This is the dim and the fleeting: meet it, and you do not see its face; follow it, and you do not see its back.
Hold fast to the ancient Way, and use it to master the things of the present. To know how things were in the beginning long ago — this is called the thread of the Way.
The masters of the Way in ancient times were subtle, mysterious, and deep beyond all knowing. Because they could not be known, I can only describe how they appeared.

Wary, like someone crossing a frozen stream in winter. Watchful, like someone alert to enemies on every side. Reserved, like a guest. Yielding, like ice on the point of melting. Plain, like an uncarved block of wood. Open, like a valley. And murky, like muddy water.

Who can let the muddy water settle and slowly grow clear? Who can stay still until the moment to stir? Whoever holds to this Way does not crave to be full; and because he is never full, he can wear out and be made new again.
Reach all the way to emptiness. Hold fast to stillness. The ten thousand things rise and stir, and I watch them return. For all their teeming growth, each one comes back to its root.

Returning to the root is stillness; this is called returning to what was fated. Returning to what was fated is the constant; to know the constant is to see clearly. Not to know it is to act blindly and bring on disaster.

Know the constant, and you grow all-embracing. All-embracing, you are impartial; impartial, you are kingly; kingly, you are like heaven; like heaven, you are one with the Way. One with the Way, you last long, and to the end of your life you come to no harm.

sections.label: Chapter 17
sections.title: The Best Ruler Is Barely Known

segments.text: The best ruler is one the people barely know is there. Next comes the ruler they love and praise. Next, the one they fear. And worst, the one they despise. Where trust runs short, it is met with distrust.
The best ruler hangs back, and is sparing of words. When the work is done and everything has run its course, the people all say: we did this ourselves.
When the great Way is abandoned, humaneness and righteousness come forward. When cleverness and sharp wits arise, great pretense follows close behind.
When the six bonds of kin fall out of harmony, filial devotion and parental love are praised. When the state sinks into disorder, loyal ministers appear.

Renounce sageliness, throw out cleverness, and the people will be better off a hundredfold. Renounce humaneness, throw out righteousness, and the people will return to devotion within their families and care for one another. Renounce ingenuity, throw out the chase after gain, and there will be no more thieves or bandits.
These three are mere ornament, and ornament is not enough. So let the people hold to something solid: see the plain and undyed, hold to the uncarved block, think little of self, and want little.

Give up learning, and you will have no more worries. Between a respectful "yes" and a careless "yeah," how much difference is there really? Between what people call good and what they call bad, how wide is the gulf that separates them?
What everyone fears must indeed be feared. But how vast and endless this all is, with no place to come to rest!

The crowd is merry and content, as if feasting at a great banquet, as if climbing a tower in spring. I alone am still, giving no sign, my desires not yet stirring, like an infant that has not yet learned to smile. I am weary and forlorn, like one with no home to return to. Everyone else has more than enough; I alone seem to have lost everything. Mine is the mind of a fool, muddled and dim.

Ordinary people are bright and clever; I alone am dull. Ordinary people are sharp and sure; I alone am clouded and confused. I drift like the restless sea; I am blown about, as if I had nowhere to settle. Everyone else has their work and their purpose; I alone am awkward and useless, like a country bumpkin. I alone am different from all the rest — for I am nourished by the Mother, the Way.
The form of great power flows from the Way alone.

And the Way itself, as a thing, is elusive and vague. Vague and elusive, yet within it are images. Elusive and vague, yet within it are things. Deep and dark, yet within it is an essence that is real; and this essence can be trusted.
From of old until now its name has never passed away, and by it we know the origin of all things. How do I know the way of all things at their origin? By this.
Yield, and remain whole. Bend, and stay straight. Empty yourself, and be filled. Wear out, and be made new. Have little, and you will gain; have much, and you will be confused.

And so the sage holds to the One, and becomes a model for the world. He does not display himself, and so he shines. He does not justify himself, and so he is known. He does not boast, and so he is given credit. He is not proud, and so he endures. It is because he does not contend that no one in the world can contend with him.
The old saying — yield, and remain whole — how could that be empty words? Truly it keeps a person whole, and brings them home.

To say little is the way of nature. A whirlwind does not last a whole morning; a downpour does not last a whole day. Who makes these things? Heaven and earth. And if even heaven and earth cannot make them last long, how much less can a person.
So one who follows the Way becomes one with the Way; one who follows its power becomes one with that power; and one who follows loss becomes one with loss.

The Way gladly receives whoever becomes one with the Way; its power gladly receives whoever becomes one with that power; and loss gladly receives whoever becomes one with loss. Where there is not trust enough, no trust is returned.
Stand on tiptoe, and you cannot keep your balance. Take great striding steps, and you cannot keep walking.

Show yourself off, and you do not shine. Insist you are right, and you are not seen for what you are. Boast of what you have done, and the credit is not given you. Be proud of yourself, and you do not last.
Seen in the light of the Way, all this is leftover food and a tumor on the body — things that everyone finds repulsive. And so whoever holds to the Way will have nothing to do with them.

sections.label: Chapter 25
sections.title: Something Formed Before Heaven and Earth

segments.text: There was something formed out of the formless, complete in itself, that came to be before heaven and earth. Silent, and without shape, it stands alone and never changes; it moves through everything and is never worn away. It can be taken for the mother of all the world.
I do not know its name. Pressed to name it, I call it the Way; and straining further, I call it Great.

Great means flowing on without end; flowing on without end means reaching far; reaching far means returning. So the Way is great, heaven is great, earth is great, and the human being is great too. In all the world there are four that are great, and the human being is one of them.
The human being follows the earth; the earth follows heaven; heaven follows the Way; and the Way follows what is natural — what is so of itself.
The heavy is the root of the light; stillness masters restlessness.

And so the sage travels all day without leaving the baggage wagon behind. Splendid sights may rise before him, yet he keeps his place, calm and aloof. How then should the lord of ten thousand chariots carry himself lightly before the world? To be light is to lose the root; to be restless is to lose your mastery.

A good traveler leaves no track. A good speaker says nothing that can be faulted. A good reckoner needs no counting rods. A good closer uses no bolt, yet what he has shut cannot be opened. A good binder uses no cord, yet what he has bound cannot be loosed.
And so the sage is always good at saving people, and abandons no one; always good at saving things, and throws nothing away. This is called following the light.

So the good are the teachers of the bad, and the bad are the raw material of the good. To think nothing of the teacher, to care nothing for the material — this, however clever you are, is to be badly lost. This is the essential mystery.
Know the masculine, but keep to the feminine, and be the ravine of the world. Be the ravine of the world, and the constant power will never leave you; you return to the state of a newborn child.
Know the white, but keep to the black, and be the model for the world. Be the model for the world, and the constant power will never fail you; you return to the limitless.
Know honor, but keep to disgrace, and be the valley of the world. Be the valley of the world, and the constant power will be complete in you; you return to the uncarved block.
When the uncarved block is split, it is made into vessels. The sage, put to use, becomes the chief of officials. And so the greatest carving cuts nothing away.

Whoever wants to take the world and shape it to his will, I see that he will not succeed. The world is a sacred vessel, not to be tampered with. Tamper with it, and you ruin it; grasp at it, and you lose it.
For things go their own way: some lead, others follow; some breathe gently, others hard; some are strong, others weak; some rise up, others fall down.
And so the sage casts off excess, casts off extravagance, casts off pride.
Whoever helps a ruler of men by the Way does not use weapons to force his will on the world. Such a course comes back on the one who takes it.
Where armies have camped, thorns and brambles grow. In the wake of great wars come years of famine.

The good commander strikes his blow and stops; he does not dare to press on and take the world by force. He strikes the blow, but does not boast of it; he strikes it, but does not brag; he strikes it, but is not proud. He strikes only because there was no other choice; he strikes, but not to force his mastery.
Things in their full strength grow old. This is what it means to be against the Way, and what is against the Way comes early to its end.

sections.label: Chapter 31
sections.title: Weapons Are Instruments of Ill Omen

segments.text: Even the finest weapons are instruments of ill omen, hated, you might say, by every living thing. And so one who has the Way does not dwell among them.

In peace the gentleman honors the left; in war he honors the right. Weapons are instruments of ill omen, not the gentleman's instruments; he takes them up only when there is no other choice. What he prizes is calm and quiet; victory brings him no joy. To find joy in it would be to delight in killing, and the one who delights in killing will never win the world.

On glad occasions the place of honor is the left; on mourning occasions, the right. In the army the second-in-command stands on the left, and the commanding general on the right — set, that is, in the place of the rites of mourning. For when a multitude of men has been killed, we should weep for them with grief and sorrow; and a victory in battle should be observed as a funeral.

The Way is eternal and has no name. The uncarved block, though small, is something no one in the world can master. If kings and lords could only hold to it, all things would come to them of their own accord.
Heaven and earth would join and let fall a sweet dew, and the people, with no one to command them, would fall into order by themselves.
Once things are cut and shaped, there are names. And once there are names, you must know when to stop. Knowing when to stop is how you come to no harm.
The Way is to the world what the rivers and streams are to the sea — everything flows down to it and home.

To know others is wisdom; to know yourself is clear sight. To master others takes force; to master yourself takes true strength. To know that you have enough is to be rich. To keep going with resolve is to have will.
Whoever does not lose his place endures. Whoever dies but is not lost lives on.
The great Way flows everywhere. It can reach out to the left and to the right.

All things depend on it for their life, and it turns none of them away. It does its work and lays no claim to it. It clothes and feeds all things, yet does not set itself up as their master. Forever without desire of its own, it can be called small. All things come home to it, yet it does not lord it over them, and so it can be called great.
Because it never makes itself out to be great, it is able to achieve its greatness.
Hold fast to the great image, and the whole world comes to you. It comes and takes no harm, but finds rest, peace, and ease.

Music and fine food make the passing traveler stop. But when the Way is put into words, it is bland and without flavor. Look for it, and there is nothing to see; listen for it, and there is nothing to hear; yet use it, and it is never used up.

If you would shrink a thing, you must first let it stretch wide. If you would weaken a thing, you must first let it grow strong. If you would lay a thing low, you must first let it rise high. If you would take a thing away, you must first give to it. This is called the subtle light.
The soft and weak overcome the hard and strong.
Fish should not leave the deep water; and the sharp tools of a state should not be put on show before the people.
The Way never forces anything, yet nothing is left undone.
If lords and kings could hold to it, all things would change of themselves.
And if, as they changed, desire began to stir, I would still it with the nameless block of uncarved wood.
The nameless uncarved block: it too is free of desire. Without desire, there is stillness, and the world settles of itself.
The highest virtue is not virtuous, and that is why it has virtue. The lowest virtue never lets go of being virtuous, and that is why it has none.
The highest virtue acts without forcing, and acts from no motive. The lowest virtue acts, and acts from a motive.

The highest humaneness acts, but from no motive. The highest righteousness acts, and from a motive. The highest ritual acts, and when no one answers it, it bares the arm and drags them along by force.
So when the Way is lost, virtue appears. When virtue is lost, humaneness appears. When humaneness is lost, righteousness appears. When righteousness is lost, ritual appears.
Ritual is the thin husk of loyalty and good faith, and the beginning of disorder. Foreknowledge is only the flower of the Way, and the beginning of folly.
And so the great person dwells in the substance, not in the husk; dwells in the fruit, not in the flower. He lets the one go and takes hold of the other.

From of old, these are the things that attained the One: heaven attained it and became clear; earth attained it and became firm; the spirits attained it and became holy; the valleys attained it and became full; all living things attained it and lived; rulers and kings attained it and became the standard for the world. It is the One that made them so.

Without it, heaven would have nothing to keep it clear, and would crack. Earth would have nothing to keep it firm, and would quake. The spirits would have nothing to make them holy, and would fade. The valleys would have nothing to keep them full, and would run dry. All living things would have nothing to keep them alive, and would die out. Rulers and kings would have nothing to keep them high, and would fall.

So the noble takes the humble as its root, and the high takes the low as its foundation. That is why rulers and kings call themselves orphaned, widowed, unworthy. Is this not because they hold the humble to be their root? Take a carriage apart piece by piece, and there is no carriage left to find. The highest renown is to have no renown. So do not wish to glitter like jade; be plain like common stone.

sections.label: Chapter 40
sections.title: Returning Is the Movement of the Way

segments.text: Returning is the movement of the Way; yielding is its use.
All things under heaven are born of being, and being is born of non-being.

When the best student hears about the Way, he sets to work and practices it with all his heart. When the middling student hears about it, he half keeps it and half lets it go. When the worst student hears about it, he laughs out loud. And if he did not laugh, it would not be the Way.

So the old sayings have it: The bright Way looks dark. The Way that goes forward looks as if it were going back. The smooth Way looks rough. The highest power looks empty, like a valley. The purest white looks stained. The broadest power looks as if it falls short. Firm, settled power looks flimsy. What is most real looks as if it could change. The great square has no corners. The great vessel is the last to be finished. The great sound can barely be heard. The great image has no shape.
The Way is hidden and has no name. Yet it is the Way alone that gives all things what they need and brings them to completion.

The Way bore the One; the One bore the Two; the Two bore the Three; and the Three bore the ten thousand things. All things carry yin on their backs and hold yang in their arms, and the blending of these breaths makes their harmony.

There is nothing people hate more than to be called orphaned, lonely, or unworthy — yet these are the very names that kings and lords take for themselves. For some things gain by being made less, and some things lose by being made more.
What others teach, I also teach: the violent and overbearing do not die a natural death. I take this as the father of my teaching.
The softest thing in the world rides down the hardest. What has no substance slips in where there is no opening. By this I know the worth of acting without forcing.
The teaching that uses no words, the good that comes of acting without forcing — few in the world ever reach them.
Your name or your self — which is dearer? Your self or your wealth — which matters more? Gaining or losing — which does you the greater harm?
So the more you love, the more it costs you; the more you hoard, the heavier the loss when it goes.
Know what is enough, and you meet no disgrace. Know when to stop, and you meet no danger. And so you endure.

Great perfection seems flawed, yet its use never wears out. Great fullness seems empty, yet its use is never used up. Great straightness seems bent. Great skill seems clumsy. Great eloquence seems to stammer.
Movement overcomes the cold; stillness overcomes the heat. Purity and stillness set the world right.
When the Way prevails in the world, the swift horses are sent back to haul dung for the fields. When the Way is cast aside, war-horses are bred out along the borders.

There is no calamity greater than not knowing when you have enough; there is no fault greater than the craving to get more. So the contentment of one who knows he has enough is contentment that lasts.
Without going out the door, you can know the world. Without looking through the window, you can see the Way of heaven. The farther you go, the less you know.
And so the sage knows without going about, understands and names things without seeing them, and accomplishes without acting.

In the pursuit of learning, something is added every day. In the pursuit of the Way, something is dropped every day. Dropped, and dropped again, until you come to acting without forcing. Act without forcing, and nothing is left undone.
The world is always won by leaving it alone. Once you start to meddle, you are not fit to win the world.

sections.label: Chapter 49
sections.title: The Sage Has No Fixed Mind

segments.text: The sage has no fixed mind of his own; he takes the mind of the people as his own.
To the good he is good; to those who are not good he is also good — and so goodness is won. The trustworthy he trusts; those who are not trustworthy he also trusts — and so trust is won.
The sage, living in the world, draws everything in and blends his mind with the world's. The people fix their eyes and ears on him, and he treats them all as his children.
We come out into life and go back into death.

Three in ten are companions of life. Three in ten are companions of death. And three in ten are those who live, yet move the whole way toward the ground of death. Why? Because they clutch too hard at living.

But I have heard that one who truly knows how to live can cross the land without meeting rhinoceros or tiger, and pass through battle without armor or weapon. The rhinoceros finds no place to gore him, the tiger no place to sink its claws, the blade no place to drive its point. Why? Because in him there is no room for death.

sections.label: Chapter 51
sections.title: The Way Gives Life, Virtue Nurtures

segments.text: The Way gives all things their life, and its virtue nurtures them. Matter gives them their shapes, and circumstance brings them to completion. So there is nothing among all things that does not honor the Way and value its virtue.
This honoring of the Way and valuing of its virtue is commanded by no one. It is always so of itself.
For the Way gives all things life and its virtue nurtures them: it rears them and raises them, it shelters them and ripens them, it feeds them and shields them.
It gives them life and does not possess them; it does the work and lays no claim to it; it leads, and does not lord it over what it leads. This is what is called the mysterious virtue.
The world had a beginning, and that beginning was the mother of all.
Once you have found the mother, you know her children. Once you know that you are her child, and hold fast to the mother in you, then to the end of your life you will meet no danger.
Stop up the openings, shut the gates, and to the end of your days your strength will never run out. Open the openings, pile up your affairs, and to the end of your days there is no saving you.
To see the small is clarity. To keep to the soft is strength.
Use the outer light, but turn back to the inner light, and you will leave no harm behind you. This is what it means to live by the constant Way.
If I had the smallest scrap of sense, I would walk the great Way, and fear only one thing — that I might stray from it.
The great Way is smooth and easy, but people love the bypaths.

The courts are swept spotless while the fields choke with weeds and the granaries stand empty. Yet some wear embroidered robes, carry sharp swords at the hip, gorge themselves on food and drink, and hoard more wealth than they could ever use. This is the robber's boast, not the Way.
What is well planted cannot be uprooted. What is firmly held cannot slip away. So from generation to generation the children will keep the rites and never let the offerings to the ancestors cease.

Cultivate the Way in yourself, and your power becomes real. Cultivate it in the family, and its power overflows. Cultivate it in the village, and its power endures. Cultivate it in the state, and its power abounds. Cultivate it in the world, and its power reaches everywhere.
So look at the self through the self, the family through the family, the village through the village, the state through the state, the world through the world.
How do I know the world is like this? By this.

sections.label: Chapter 55
sections.title: Full of Virtue, Like a Newborn Child

segments.text: One full of virtue is like a newborn child. Stinging insects do not sting it, fierce beasts do not seize it, birds of prey do not strike it.

Its bones are soft and its sinews weak, yet its grip is firm. It does not yet know the union of female and male, yet its little member stirs — such is the perfection of its vital essence. It can cry all day without growing hoarse — such is the perfection of its harmony.
To know harmony is to know the constant. To know the constant is clarity. To force more life is to court ill omen. For the mind to drive the breath is to overstrain.
Things in their full strength grow old. This is what it means to be against the Way, and what is against the Way comes early to its end.

sections.label: Chapter 56
sections.title: Those Who Know Do Not Speak

segments.text: Those who know do not speak; those who speak do not know.
Block the openings, shut the gates. Blunt the sharp edges, untie the tangles, soften the glare, settle into the dust. This is called the mysterious union.
Such a one cannot be drawn close or held at a distance, cannot be helped or harmed, cannot be honored or disgraced. And so they are honored by all the world.

sections.label: Chapter 57
sections.title: Win the World by Not Meddling

segments.text: Govern the state with what is straight and ordinary. Wage war with surprise. But win the world by not meddling.

How do I know it works this way? By this. The more prohibitions there are in the land, the poorer the people grow. The more sharp weapons the people have, the deeper the state falls into disorder. The more clever and cunning people become, the more strange things start to happen. The more laws and decrees are posted up, the more thieves and robbers there are.

So the sage says: I act without forcing, and the people transform themselves. I love stillness, and the people right themselves. I do not meddle, and the people grow prosperous on their own. I have no desires, and the people return on their own to the uncarved block.
When the government is dull and unobtrusive, the people stay honest and whole. When the government is sharp and prying, the people grow crafty and broken.

Misfortune is what fortune leans on; fortune is where misfortune hides. Who knows where it all ends? There is no fixed standard. What is right turns strange, and what is good turns monstrous. Long, long has mankind been lost in this.
So the sage is square-edged but cuts no one, sharp-cornered but wounds no one, straight but never severe, bright but not dazzling.
In governing people and in serving heaven, nothing is better than restraint.

It is only by restraint that you yield early to the Way; and yielding early means storing up an ever deeper store of power. With that deep store of power, there is nothing you cannot overcome; and when there is nothing you cannot overcome, no one can know your limit. The one whose limit no one knows is fit to hold the state.
Hold to the mother of the state, and you may last long. This is what it means to have deep roots and a firm base — the way of long life and lasting vision.
Governing a great state is like cooking a small fish.

Let the world be governed by the Way, and the spirits of the dead lose their power to haunt. It is not that they have no such power, but that their power does no harm to the people. And it is not only that their power does no harm — neither does the sage who rules do any harm.
Since neither does harm, the power of each flows back and gathers in the people.
